$comment: What a thing does at a temperature: where it melts, and where it boils, breaks down or turns straight to gas. Loam's own facts carry a melting point for only seven things, so the tube could not melt copper. Each row here is sourced on its own line. Melting is a change of STATE, not of substance: molten copper is still copper, and the engine keeps the thing's id and makes it a liquid. Where Loam has a recipe for the change (gold -> molten gold) Loam's recipe wins and these are not used.

$fields.range: low and high, for a mixture or alloy that has no single point
$fields.decomposes: it breaks down before it melts
$fields.sublimes: it goes straight from solid to gas
$fields.note: one plain sentence on why it is not a single clean number

actinium.note: The melting point is estimated and the boiling point extrapolated, as actinium is too scarce and radioactive to measure easily.

alnico.note: Wikipedia gives this range for Alnico 3, and the other alnico grades differ with their mix.

americium.note: Wikipedia marks the boiling point as calculated rather than measured.

basalt.note: A mixture of minerals, so it melts over a range.

berkelium.note: Both figures are for the beta form of the metal.

beryllium_copper.note: The alloy is pasty between its solidus at 866 C and its liquidus at 982 C.

bismuth_telluride.note: No boiling point is listed for this compound.

blister_copper.note: Blister copper is about 98 percent copper, so it melts very close to copper's own point.

brass.note: Brass melts across a range that shifts with the proportion of copper to zinc.

bronze.note: Wikipedia gives about 950 C, varying with the ratio of copper to tin, without stating the bounds of that variation.

butter.note: A mixture of fats, so it softens over a range.

californium.note: Wikipedia marks the boiling point as an estimation.

cast_iron.note: Carbon near 4.3 percent drops iron's melting point to about 1130 C, far below pure iron's 1538 C.

citric_acid.note: It melts and then breaks down above about 175 degrees.

copernicium.note: Both figures are predictions carrying about ten degrees of uncertainty.

copper_cathode.note: Electrorefined cathode copper is refined copper, so it melts at copper's own point.

curium.note: Wikipedia's infobox and body text disagree, the body giving 1344 C and 3556 C instead.

einsteinium.note: Wikipedia marks the boiling point as estimated.

enriched_uranium.note: Enrichment changes only the isotope mix, so enriched uranium metal melts and boils like ordinary uranium.

fermium.note: The melting point is predicted, not measured, and no boiling point is known.

ferrovanadium.note: Wikipedia gives one figure although the vanadium content ranges from 35 to 85 percent.

flerovium.note: The melting point is a prediction with about fifty degrees of uncertainty, and no boiling point is given.

francium.note: Too little francium has ever existed at once to measure, so both figures are estimates.

galvanized_iron.note: Galvanised iron is steel under a zinc coat, so the coating runs at about 420 C while the steel beneath holds past 1500 C.

glass.note: Glass has no melting point: it softens gradually, which is why it can be blown.

granite.note: A mixture of minerals, so it melts over a range.

inconel_625.note: This nickel superalloy melts between a solidus of 1290 C and a liquidus of 1350 C.

laminations.note: Laminations are stacked strips of silicon electrical steel, which melts at about 1500 C.

lawrencium.note: The melting point is predicted, not measured, and no boiling point is known.

lead_came.note: Came for stained glass is usually plain lead strip, so it melts at lead's own point.

limestone.note: It does not melt at ordinary pressure: it breaks down into quicklime and carbon dioxide first.

livermorium.note: Wikipedia gives extrapolated bands rather than points, 364 to 507 C for melting and 762 to 862 C for boiling.

mendelevium.note: The melting point is predicted, not measured, and no boiling point is known.

moscovium.note: Both figures are predictions, as moscovium has only ever existed as a few atoms.

nak_alloy.note: The eutectic of 77 percent potassium and 23 percent sodium is liquid from -12.6 C up to 785 C.

neptunium.note: The boiling point is extrapolated from vapour pressure rather than measured.

nichrome.note: Wikipedia gives about 1400 C for C-grade nichrome, without stating bounds for other grades.

nickel_sulfate.note: The anhydrous salt breaks down above about 640 C instead of boiling, while the green hexahydrate melts at only 53 C.

nihonium.note: Both figures are predictions, as nihonium has only ever existed as a few atoms.

nobelium.note: The melting point is predicted, not measured, and no boiling point is known.

oganesson.note: Both figures are predictions, as oganesson has only ever existed as a few atoms.

pig_iron.note: Pig iron's roughly 4 percent carbon drops its melting point to about 1130 C, which is why a blast furnace can tap it as a liquid.

promethium.note: The boiling point is an estimate, as promethium has no stable isotope and is handled only in tiny amounts.

protactinium.note: Wikipedia flags the boiling point as uncertain.

radium.note: Wikipedia marks radium's melting point as disputed.

rail.note: A rail is rolled carbon steel, which softens over a range rather than melting at one point.

rutherfordium.note: Both figures are predictions, as rutherfordium has only ever existed as a few atoms.

samarium.note: Wikipedia's infobox gives 1900 C for the boiling point while its body text gives 1794 C.

sand.note: Sand is mostly quartz, and melts near where pure silica does.

silver_carbonate.note: It begins breaking down at about 120 C, before its 218 C melting point is reached.

solder.note: Soft solders are a whole family melting anywhere from 90 to 450 C, and the single figure here is common 60/40 tin-lead.

stainless_steel.note: Stainless steel melts over a range that depends on which alloy it is.

steel.note: Carbon steel softens over a range rather than at one point, and this range is the one Wikipedia gives for A36 structural steel.

sugar.note: It does not melt cleanly: it caramelises as it goes.

tarnish.note: The black tarnish on silver is silver sulfide, which melts at 836 C.

tennessine.note: The melting point is predicted only as a band from 350 to 550 C, and the boiling point is also a prediction.

tin_silver_solder.note: The tin-silver eutectic melts at a single point rather than over a range.

titanium_nitride.note: No boiling point is listed for this ceramic.

tungsten_carbide.note: Wikipedia gives the melting point as a band from 2785 to 2830 C.

wax.note: A mixture of hydrocarbons, so it softens over a range.

wrought_iron.note: Wrought iron was always worked hot rather than melted, since with almost no carbon it melts as high as pure iron.
